lesson.title: Times tables, 2–12
lesson.body:
Every multi-digit product you will ever do mentally is a stack of single-digit products. If 7 × 8 costs you a second of hesitation, 47 × 68 costs you four of them plus the strain of holding intermediate results. The goal here is instant recall — under a second, no counting up, no rederiving.

There are only 55 facts once you notice a × b = b × a and drop the trivial ×1 and ×10. Most of them collapse to a few patterns:

  • ×2, ×4, ×8: double once, twice, three times.
  • ×5: half of ×10. ×9: ×10 minus one copy (the digits sum to 9).
  • ×11: repeat the digit. ×12: ×10 plus ×2.
  • Neighbours of squares: (n−1)(n+1) = n² − 1, so 6 × 8 = 49 − 1 = 48.

The genuinely hard ones are the "middle" facts: 6 × 7 = 42, 6 × 8 = 48, 7 × 7 = 49, 7 × 8 = 56 (5-6-7-8), 7 × 9 = 63, 8 × 8 = 64. Use the derivation when you miss, but the aim is to stop needing it: say the fact aloud, then retype it from memory.

lesson.title: Teens × one digit
lesson.body:
Products like 17 × 6 = 102 or 14 × 8 = 112 turn up constantly: in percentages, in unit conversions, inside every two-digit multiplication. They are just past the times table, so it pays to know them by heart rather than compute them each time.

The derivation is always the same: split off the ten. 17 × 6 = 10 × 6 + 7 × 6 = 60 + 42 = 102. Some are faster another way:

  • 19 × m = 20 × m − m: 19 × 7 = 140 − 7 = 133.
  • 15 × m = 10m plus half of 10m: 15 × 8 = 80 + 40 = 120.
  • 18 × m can also be 20m − 2m: 18 × 7 = 140 − 14 = 126.

Practise until the answer arrives before the derivation does. The landmarks worth noticing: 12 × 8 = 96, 13 × 7 = 91, 14 × 7 = 98, 16 × 6 = 96, 17 × 6 = 102, 18 × 6 = 108, 19 × 9 = 171, and 16 × 8 = 128 and 16 × 4 = 64 (powers of 2).

lesson.title: Squares 11–30
lesson.body:
Squares are the backbone of fast multiplication. With them, any product of two numbers that are close together becomes a subtraction: a × b = m² − d², where m is their midpoint and d half their gap. So 23 × 27 = 25² − 2² = 625 − 4 = 621, and 18 × 22 = 400 − 4 = 396. They also give you square roots for free: √500 ≈ 22.4 because 22² = 484 and 23² = 529.

Three derivations to fall back on while memorizing:

  • Ends in 5: multiply the tens digit by the next integer, append 25. 25² = 2 × 3 | 25 = 625.
  • Teens: (n + units) × 10 + units². 17² = 240 + 49 = 289.
  • Round to a ten: n² = (n − d)(n + d) + d². 28² = 30 × 26 + 4 = 784.

Worth knowing cold: 16² = 256 and 32² = 1024 (powers of two), 24² = 576, 27² = 729 = 9³, and 29² = 900 − 60 + 1 = 841 (so 31² = 900 + 60 + 1 = 961).

lesson.title: Cubes
lesson.body:
Cubes matter for volumes (a 12-inch cube is 1728 in³), for cube roots, and for recognising numbers: if you see 343 or 729 or 1331 you should feel the 7, 9 or 11 behind it. Knowing them also makes cube roots fast: ∛600 is between 8 (512) and 9 (729), roughly 8.4.

Each cube is the square times the base again: 7³ = 7 × 49 = 343, 12³ = 12 × 144 = 1728. A few have extra hooks:

  • 4³ = 64 and 8³ = 512 are powers of two (2⁶, 2⁹).
  • 5³ = 125 = 1000/8, the reason 1/8 = 0.125.
  • 9³ = 729 = 27² = 3⁶.
  • 11³ = 1331 is row 3 of Pascal's triangle.
  • 6³ = 216 = 3³ + 4³ + 5³.

Also notice the last digits: cubes of 1–9 end in 1, 8, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 9 — every digit appears once, so the last digit of a perfect cube tells you the last digit of its root.

cards.note: 12 × 144 = 1728 — cubic inches in a cubic foot.

lesson.title: Powers of two
lesson.body:
The single most useful fact here is 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≈ 10³. It converts between doubling and powers of ten: 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹, 2⁴⁰ ≈ 10¹². So 2³⁴ = 2⁴ × 2³⁰ ≈ 16 × 10⁹. It is also why log10 2 ≈ 0.3 (ten doublings ≈ three decades).

Powers of two show up everywhere: doubling times and compound growth, computer memory, halving in binary search, and the "rule of 70" problems later on. They also give you reciprocals: 1/8 = 0.125, 1/16 = 0.0625, 1/32 = 0.03125.

How to learn them:

  • Up to 2¹⁰ = 1024, just double: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024.
  • Above that, split off 2¹⁰: 2¹³ = 8 × 1024 = 8192; 2¹⁶ = 64 × 1024 = 65 536.
  • Rhythm helps: 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16 384, 32 768, 65 536 — say them as a chant.

Negative powers are just halvings of 1: 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.03125.

cards.note: 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≈ 10³ — the bridge between binary and decimal.

lesson.title: Small-integer powers
lesson.body:
Powers of 3, 5, 6 and 7 come up in probability (6⁵ = 7776 dice outcomes), combinatorics, compound growth, and in checking logarithms: 3¹⁰ = 59 049 ≈ 6 × 10⁴ tells you 10 × log 3 ≈ 4.77, i.e. log 3 ≈ 0.477. Recognising them also lets you spot that 2401 is 7⁴ or 15 625 is 5⁶ = 125².

Build each from one you already know rather than memorizing in isolation:

  • Square a square: 3⁸ = 81² = 6561, 6⁴ = 36² = 1296, 7⁴ = 49² = 2401.
  • One more factor: 3⁷ = 3 × 729 = 2187, 7⁵ = 7 × 2401 = 16 807.
  • Powers of 5 are powers of 10 over powers of 2: 5⁶ = 10⁶ / 64 = 15 625.
  • Powers of 4 and 8 are powers of 2: 4⁵ = 2¹⁰, 8⁴ = 2¹².
  • Powers of 11 follow Pascal's triangle: 121, 1331, 14 641.

The 3-chain is worth chanting: 9, 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187, 6561, 19 683, 59 049.

lesson.title: Reciprocals and common fractions
lesson.body:
Division is slow; multiplication is fast. Knowing reciprocals lets you turn one into the other: ÷ 8 is × 0.125, ÷ 7 is × 0.1429, ÷ 16 is × 0.0625. So 350 ÷ 7 is easy anyway, but 37 ÷ 7 ≈ 37 × 0.143 ≈ 5.29, and 91 ÷ 16 = 91 × 0.0625 ≈ 5.69. Fractions are also how you convert percentages and ratios in your head: 5/8 = 62.5 %, 3/7 ≈ 42.9 %.

Type answers to 3 decimal places (or exactly, for the ones that terminate).

  • Eighths and sixteenths are multiples of 0.125 and 0.0625.
  • Ninths: n/9 = 0.nnn…. Elevenths: n/11 repeats 9n (3/11 = 0.2727…).
  • Sevenths all use the cyclic digits 142857: 1/7 = 0.142857…, 2/7 = 0.285714…, 3/7 = 0.428571…. Start at the right place by estimating (3/7 is a bit under 0.43).
  • Halve to get the next: 1/6 from 1/3, 1/12 from 1/6, 1/14 from 1/7.
  • Odd ones via a near multiple: 13 × 77 = 1001 so 1/13 ≈ 0.077; 17 × 6 = 102 so 1/17 ≈ 0.0588.

cards.note: Cyclic 142857. Every n/7 is a rotation of the same six digits.
Rotate 142857 to start at the next-biggest digit: 0.285714…

lesson.title: Common logarithms: the anchors
lesson.body:
With a handful of logs you can take the log of any number by factoring, and the antilog of any exponent by reversing the table. That is the engine behind fast estimation of products, powers and roots: multiply by adding logs.

The four to know cold: log 2 = 0.301, log 3 = 0.477, log 7 = 0.845, and log e = 0.434. Everything else follows:

  • log 4 = 2 × 0.301 = 0.602, log 8 = 0.903, log 5 = 1 − 0.301 = 0.699.
  • log 6 = 0.301 + 0.477 = 0.778, log 9 = 0.954, log 1.5 = 0.477 − 0.301 = 0.176.

Example: log 4200 = 3 + log 4.2 = 3 + log 6 + log 7 − 1 = 3 + 0.778 + 0.845 − 1 = 3.623.

The reverse cards are the same facts read backwards: 100.3 ≈ 2, 100.6 ≈ 4, 100.7 ≈ 5, 100.9 ≈ 8, plus 100.5 = √10 = 3.162 and 100.1 ≈ 1.26. So 104.7 ≈ 5 × 10⁴ instantly.

Answer logs to 3 decimal places and antilogs to about 3 significant figures.

cards.note: log e = 1/ln 10 = 0.434 — the ln → log conversion factor.

lesson.title: Natural logarithms: the anchors
lesson.body:
Natural logs are the language of growth and decay: continuous interest, half-lives, doubling times, entropy, anything with ex. Like common logs, a few anchors generate the rest by factoring.

Know cold: ln 2 = 0.693, ln 3 = 1.099, ln 10 = 2.303. Then:

  • ln 5 = ln 10 − ln 2 = 1.609; ln 4 = 1.386; ln 8 = 2.079; ln 6 = 1.792; ln 9 = 2.197.
  • ln 7 ≈ 1.946 (half of ln 49, a bit under half of ln 50).
  • Small x: ln(1 + x) ≈ x − x²/2, so ln 1.1 ≈ 0.095, ln 1.05 ≈ 0.049.
  • Conversions: ln x = 2.303 × log x, and log x = 0.434 × ln x.

Example: a quantity growing 7 % a year doubles in about ln 2 / 0.07 ≈ 0.693 / 0.07 ≈ 10 years — the "rule of 70". And ln 30 = ln 3 + ln 10 = 1.099 + 2.303 = 3.401.

Answer to 3 decimal places.

cards.note: 0.693 — the rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 / (% rate).
−ln 2 = −0.693: ln of a reciprocal is the negative.
= log<sub>10</sub> e = 0.434. ln → log: multiply by 0.434.
= log<sub>2</sub> e = 1.443. ln → log₂: multiply by 1.443.

lesson.title: Powers of e
lesson.body:
Exponentials are logs read backwards, and they appear directly in compound growth, radioactive decay, probability (the Poisson e−λ), and physics. These anchors let you evaluate ex for any x: split x into a piece you know plus a small remainder.

  • e = 2.718, e² = 7.389, e³ ≈ 20.09, e⁵ ≈ 148.
  • e0.693 = 2, e2.303 = 10 (the natural-log anchors reversed).
  • Negatives are reciprocals: e−1 = 0.368, e−2 = 0.135, e−3 ≈ 0.05.
  • Small x: ex ≈ 1 + x + x²/2, so e0.1 ≈ 1.105.

Example: e3.7 = e3 × e0.7 ≈ 20.09 × 2.01 ≈ 40.4 (0.7 ≈ ln 2 + 0.007). Or think in decades: ex = 100.434x, so e10 = 104.34 ≈ 2.2 × 10⁴.

Answer to about 3 significant figures (within 1 %).

lesson.title: Constants and roots
lesson.body:
These numbers recur in geometry, physics and statistics, and in every trig value: sin 60° is √3/2, a circle's area is πr², a normal curve's peak is 1/√(2π). Knowing them to four significant figures means your estimates are never limited by a fuzzy constant.

  • √2 = 1.414, √3 = 1.732, √5 = 2.236. Then √6 = √2√3 = 2.449, √8 = 2√2 = 2.828, √10 = 3.162.
  • π = 3.1416, so 2π = 6.283, π/2 = 1.571, π² = 9.870, 1/π = 0.318, √π = 1.772.
  • e = 2.71828, 1/e = 0.368. φ = 1.618 = (1 + √5)/2, and 1/φ = φ − 1.
  • Cube roots: ∛2 = 1.26, ∛10 = 2.154.

Memorize by checking: square your answer (1.732² = 2.9998), or derive from a neighbour (1/√2 = √2/2). Use the mnemonics in the card notes for π and e.

Answer to 4 significant figures.

cards.note: 3.14159 — "How I wish I could calculate pi" (word lengths 3.141592).

lesson.title: Special angles and radians
lesson.body:
Every trig estimate starts from a nearby known angle: sin 37° is "a bit more than sin 30° = 0.5", tan 70° is "a bit less than tan 75° = 3.73". These values are your grid.

All of them come from two triangles. The 45-45-90 triangle (sides 1, 1, √2) gives sin 45° = cos 45° = √2/2 = 0.7071. The 30-60-90 triangle (half an equilateral, sides 1, √3, 2) gives sin 30° = ½, sin 60° = √3/2 = 0.866, tan 30° = 1/√3 = 0.577, tan 60° = √3. Cosine is sine of the complement: cos θ = sin(90° − θ).

  • 15° and 75°: sin 15° = (√6 − √2)/4 = 0.2588, cos 15° = 0.9659, tan 15° = 2 − √3 = 0.268, tan 75° = 2 + √3 = 3.732.
  • 18° and 36° involve the golden ratio: sin 18° = 0.309, cos 36° = φ/2 = 0.809.

Radians: 1 rad = 57.30°, 1° = 0.01745 rad. Multiply degrees by π/180: 30° = 0.524, 45° = 0.785, 60° = 1.047, 90° = 1.571. For small angles sin x ≈ tan x ≈ x (in radians): sin 3° ≈ 3 × 0.01745 = 0.052.

cards.note: Half an equilateral triangle: opposite = ½ hypotenuse.
180/π = 57.30°. (sin x ≈ x works because 1° is tiny: 0.01745 rad.)
